history.summary: Apache has released security updates for a critical Roller flaw tracked as CVE-2026-129448 that is being actively exploited in the wild. The vulnerability, affecting versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4, allows unauthenticated remote code execution via deserialization of untrusted data in the XML-RPC endpoint before authentication. Apache recommends upgrading to Roller 6.1.6 or later, and admins unable to upgrade can temporarily mitigate by setting "enabledForExtensions" to "false" in WEB-INF/web.xml and removing the "/roller-services/xmlrpc" servlet mapping.Fix: Upgrade to Apache Roller 6.1.6 or later, which disables extension types and rejects malicious XML-RPC requests, or apply the temporary workaround by setting "enabledForExtensions" to "false" in WEB-INF/web.xml, removing the "/roller-services/xmlrpc" servlet mapping, and restarting Roller.

history.title: Hackers Exploiting Critical Puppet RCE Flaw Affecting Enterprise Management Servers
history.text: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Tuesday added a critical security flaw impacting Perforce Puppet, an enterprise infrastructure-as-code (IaC) and configuration management platform, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing reports of active exploitation. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-115731 (CVSS score: 9.4), is a case of deserialization of untrusted data that could result in remote code execution. "Perforce Puppet Enterprise contains a deserialization of untrusted data vulnerability in Puppet's report-processing code that allows a client with any CA-signed agent certificate to execute arbitrary code on the Puppet Server as the service user by submitting a report containing a crafted rich-data type through a PUT request," CISA said. "If the certificate authority automatically signs requests without strong verification, an unauthenticated network attacker can obtain a valid certificate and exploit the vulnerability." The shortcoming impacts the following versions - - Puppet Enterprise 2026.0.0 before 2026.0.1 - Puppet Enterprise 2025.0.0 before 2025.12.1 - Puppet Enterprise 2023.8.0 before 2023.8.13 - Puppet Core 9.0.0 before 9.1.3 - Puppet Core 8.x before 8.22.2 It was addressed by Perforce Software on November 3, 2026, in the following versions - - Puppet Enterprise 2026.0.1 (Puppet Core 9.1.3) - Puppet Enterprise 2025.12.1 (Puppet Core 8.22.2) - Puppet Enterprise 2023.8.13 (Puppet Core 8.22.2) - Puppet Core 9.1.3 - Puppet Core 8.22.2 It's worth noting that the issue also affects OpenVox, an open-source implementation of Puppet, and has been resolved in the following versions - - OpenVox Agent 9.3.0 and 8.32.0 - OpenVox Server 9.2.0 and 8.18.0 Alain Rödel, a security researcher at Neodyme AG, has been credited with discovering and reporting CVE-2026-115731 along with CVE-2026-115732 (CVSS score: 9.0), a critical certificate-name authorization bypass affecting both Puppet and OpenVox. The issues were discovered with artificial intelligence (AI) assistance and precise steering, the German cybersecurity company added. "The impact highly depends on the Puppet server configuration and the orchestration protocols used, if any are enabled at all," Neodyme said in a report published this month. "Independent of the configuration, an attacker with RCE on a Puppet server can grab the CA signing keys and impersonate other hosts." "Puppet is a powerful software, often with full access to a fleet of systems in a corporate network. Remote Code Execution on such a central and important system can lead to worst-case scenarios: Deployment of ransomware, mass data exfiltration, and potentially lateral movement to other parts of the network." As of writing, there are no details on how the vulnerability is being weaponized in the wild. However, a Reddit user named transdimensia noted in a November 4 post that it was being exploited shortly after public disclosure. "After finding a severely misconfigured CA in my fleet, I traced the actions backwards on a [CVE-2026-]115731 intrusion," the user said. Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are advised to apply the fixes by December 1, 2026, to secure their networks under Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk.
history.summary: CISA added CVE-2026-115731 (CVSS 9.4) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog due to active exploitation of a deserialization flaw in Perforce Puppet's report-processing code that allows remote code execution via crafted PUT requests. Perforce Software released fixes on November 3, 2026, for affected Puppet Enterprise and Core versions, as well as OpenVox implementations. Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies must apply the fixes by December 1, 2026, under Binding Operational Directive 26-04.

history.title: Java4Shell Flaw (CVE-2026-114938) Enables Pre-Auth RCE in Jira, Jenkins, Keycloak and More
history.text: A Java flaw called Java4Shell can let attackers without an account run their own code on Jira, Jenkins, Keycloak, and three other widely used applications, says Calif, the security research firm that disclosed it this week. The flaw is present in Java 17.0.6 and later, and the vulnerable code runs only on x86-64 Intel and AMD chips that support the AVX-512 VBMI feature. Tracked as CVE-2026-114938, the fix was released today by Oracle and the OpenJDK project, whose open-source code underpins Java builds from many vendors. Amazon has fixed its Corretto Java builds, but Red Hat is still preparing fixes for its own. The researchers are holding back their attack code for the six applications, and other labs have so far reproduced crashes and a memory leak but not the code execution. Canada's Cyber Center said this week that it was not aware of any attacks exploiting the flaw. Servers often decode Base64-encoded data, such as HTTP Basic login headers, SAML artifacts, and CSRF tokens, before checking whether a user is logged in. That is how an attacker without an account can exploit the flaw. The flaw is in a faster version of Java's Base64 decoder that runs on chips with AVX-512 VBMI. Java switches to it after compiling the decoder for speed, which it does for code that runs often. A malformed string that ends with an extra = makes this decoder write 62 or 63 bytes past the end of its output. Java rejects the string, but only after the write. The bytes written past the end are fixed, so an attacker controls only where they land. For that reason, early readings of the source code had pointed to a crash rather than code execution, as The Hacker News noted in an earlier report yesterday. The attacks worked without a login under the default settings of Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate, and with a login on Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker, Calif says in its technical write-up. The researchers' lists are incomplete, and they rate the flaw as 9.2 out of 10 under CVSS 4.0. They get past the fixed bytes by arranging the server's memory so that the overflow expands a neighboring array. They then use that array to write bytes of their choosing and a second array to read back from memory, a step they call JavaBleed. From there, the researchers say, the attack reaches the parts of Java that run code. There is no single exploit that works everywhere. Each target requires its own memory layout and timing, and some attacks are sensitive to network delays. A proxy that waits for complete requests, as nginx does by default, blocks some attacks but not all. A failed attempt can crash Java, and an attacker can often try again. Security company Upwind reproduced the memory corruption on an AWS server with an Intel Ice Lake chip, where it damaged the next object in memory and eventually crashed Java, according to its lab results. Blackpoint Cyber's Adversary Pursuit Group crashed a test Spring Boot application by sending about 28,300 malformed login requests over roughly 20 seconds, without ever logging in. The group also used the JavaBleed step in a local test to read a secret stored next to the overflow, which worked in all 30 runs. It did not reproduce remote code execution, its test results show. Oracle scores the flaw 8.1 out of 10 under CVSS 3.1, rating it hard to exploit but requiring no login. The description in its CVE record says, "Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in takeover of Oracle Java SE." Red Hat also rates it as requiring no login, with a preliminary score of 9.8 out of 10. Amazon scores it 8.8 out of 10 and describes the risk in its Amazon Linux entry as "a JVM crash for unauthenticated users or, in certain application environments, code execution by an authenticated low-privileged user." Canada's Cyber Centre also describes the flaw as exploitable remotely without authentication in its government alert. The flaw was not in the KEV catalog of exploited vulnerabilities, kept by the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), when The Hacker News checked it today. Who Is Exposed The vulnerable code is in Java 17.0.6 and later on the Java 17 line, and in Java 21, 25, and 27. Standard Java 8 and Java 11 do not contain it, but the Java SE 8 Performance Pack build 8u511b33-perf is affected. GraalVM for JDK 17.0.21.0.3, GraalVM for JDK 21.0.13.0.3, and GraalVM Enterprise Edition 21.3.20.0.3 are also affected. It runs only on x86-64 chips that support AVX-512 VBMI. These include Intel Xeon Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids, and Granite Rapids chips, as well as AMD Zen 4 or newer chips. ARM64 chips do not run it. Because the vulnerable code runs only on these chips, the same container image can run it on one server and not on another. On Linux, this command shows whether a server's chip has the four features the vulnerable code needs, and all four must appear in its output: grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E '^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$' The attacker also needs malformed Base64 to reach Java's standard decoder, through paths such as the login headers and tokens described earlier. Calif also says a Java program that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server can be compromised, even if the program runs no service of its own. The exploit for this came from another researcher, samczsun, and the researchers have not published how it reaches the decoder. Fixes and Workarounds The OpenJDK project's vulnerability advisory lists the flaw as fixed in this week's releases, and Oracle's security advisory lists the affected versions of its builds. For Oracle Java, the fixed builds are the new .1 releases in the table, all released this week. The release notes for 17.0.21.1 say it includes the update's security fixes, and the notes for 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 and 27.0.1.1 say the same. For the Java 8 Performance Pack, the latest build is 8u513, available in both standard and Performance Pack versions. For GraalVM, the November security releases are GraalVM for JDK 17.0.21.1, GraalVM for JDK 21.0.13.1, and GraalVM Enterprise Edition 21.3.20.1. The Corretto changelog for 17.0.21.1.2 lists the flaw as fixed, as do the changelogs for the new 21, 25, and 27 builds. Amazon Linux also marks its Corretto 17, 21, 25 and 27 packages as fixed. Azul's November update fixes the flaw in Zulu 17, 21, 25 and 27, according to its Zulu release notes. Red Hat has not yet released fixes for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8, 9 and 10, or for its OpenJDK 17, 21 and 25 builds, according to its security bulletin. Containers based on its images need to be rebuilt once updated images are out. SAP released SapMachine 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, and 27.0.1.1 this week, but their release pages do not specify what they fix. Eclipse Temurin, the Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, and BellSoft Liberica had not listed fixed builds when The Hacker News checked today. Products that bundle their own Java runtime need an update from the product's maker. After updating, restart Java services, and rebuild and redeploy container images so the running process uses the new build. If you cannot update yet, start the JVM with one of these flags, and remove it once the fixed build is installed: - -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics turns off only the faster Base64 code, which removes the vulnerable path and leaves other AVX-512 speedups in place. - -XX:UseAVX=2 turns off AVX-512 entirely. Use it only on x86-64 servers, because Java on ARM64 does not recognize it and will fail to start. In Upwind's lab, both flags stopped the overflow on every affected version it tested. The company warns that another flag, -XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock, stops Java from starting when it is used on its own. To spot attempts, it suggests checking for the signs below, while warning that none of them proves a compromise and that their absence does not prove a server is safe: - Base64 tokens of 32 characters or more that end in = and whose length is not a multiple of 4, especially in Authorization headers - Bursts of IllegalArgumentException errors from java.util.Base64$Decoder - Unexplained hs_err_pid crash logs or bursts of restarts A malformed input that triggers the overflow was posted publicly on September 9, in a proposed fix submitted to OpenJDK's code repository as a pull request. The proposal described an overflow in the same AVX-512 Base64 decoder code. Its author closed it without merging it in early November, after an automated notice that it had been inactive for more than eight weeks.
history.summary: A Java buffer overflow flaw tracked as CVE-2026-114938 allows pre-auth remote code execution on x86-64 systems with AVX-512 VBMI across Jira, Jenkins, Keycloak and other widely used applications. The vulnerability stems from a malformed Base64 string ending in `=` that overflows the optimized decoder, and attackers can chain this with memory manipulation to expand a neighboring array and read/write arbitrary bytes, a technique researchers call JavaBleed. Oracle and OpenJDK have released fixes this week, and vendors including Amazon Corretto, Azul Zulu, and SAP SapMachine have issued updated builds, with workarounds available via JVM flags `-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics` or `-XX:UseAVX=2` to disable the vulnerable code path.

history.title: CISA Adds Four Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
history.text: CISA Adds Four Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. - CVE-2024-10441 Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM) Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output Vulnerability - CVE-2026-40217 BerriAI LiteLLM Unprotected Alternate Channel Vulnerability - CVE-2026-90436 Apache Axis Unsafe Reflection Vulnerability - CVE-2026-90817 Vanderbilt University Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) Code Injection Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance. This product is provided subject to this Notification and this Privacy & Use policy.
history.summary: CISA added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog based on evidence of active exploitation: CVE-2024-10441 (Synology DiskStation Manager), CVE-2026-40217 (BerriAI LiteLLM), CVE-2026-90436 (Apache Axis), and CVE-2026-90817 (Vanderbilt REDCap). These vulnerabilities are recognized as frequent attack vectors posing significant risks to the federal enterprise, with Binding Operational Directive 26-04 requiring FCEB agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities on publicly exposed assets that grant total control post-exploitation. CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and will continue adding vulnerabilities meeting its criteria, which require a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

history.title: F5 Warns 6 Critical BIG-IP Flaws Can Crash Traffic in Specific Setups, May Allow RCE
history.text: Six critical vulnerabilities in F5 BIG-IP allow an attacker to crash the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) without logging in, disrupting traffic until the TMM restarts. Each flaw needs a specific setup on a virtual server: an iRule that uses a particular command, or an APM policy that includes two particular kinds of agent. F5, which makes BIG-IP, disclosed the flaws today and says they may also allow remote code execution. The company has released engineering hotfixes and lists no workaround. The company rates all six 9.8 under CVSS v3.1 and 9.3 under CVSS v4.0. They are stack-based buffer overflows in BIG-IP's data plane, the part that processes almost all of its network traffic. The management side is not exposed, according to the company. None of the company's advisories says the flaws have been exploited. WatchTowr researcher Sina Kheirkhah reported four, and the company found the other two itself. Five of the flaws are in iRules, a BIG-IP feature that administrators use to manage traffic, and one is in BIG-IP's APM module. Some also affect BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes and BIG-IP CNF, part of the company's BIG-IP Cloud-Native Edition. Each flaw needs the setup listed below on a virtual server: - CVE-2026-123637: an APM per-request policy that includes both the Client Information agent and Endpoint Security agents. Affects BIG-IP APM only. - CVE-2026-121805: an iRule that uses PEM::subscriber on client traffic. Affects BIG-IP PEM, BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes and, as of today, BIG-IP CNF. - CVE-2026-120292: an HTTP profile and an iRule that uses MR::message route. Affects BIG-IP (all modules) and BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes. - CVE-2026-120285: an HTTP profile and an iRule that uses PSC::ip_address. Affects BIG-IP (all modules), BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes and, as of today, BIG-IP CNF. - CVE-2026-116953: an iRule that uses GENERICMESSAGE::route on client traffic. Affects BIG-IP (all modules) and BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes. - CVE-2026-120722: an iRule that uses DNS::scrape on client traffic. Affects BIG-IP DNS and BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes. The company's advisory lists BIG-IP CNF as not vulnerable, but its CVE record, updated today, lists CNF as affected. F5's security notification lists the 22 advisories it published today, including 10 for NGINX. For the six critical flaws, the only fixes are engineering hotfixes, builds that the company issues between its normal software releases. No scheduled release is listed as a fix, and the advisories provide no workaround until a hotfix is installed. The company warns that "engineering hotfixes do not undergo the extensive QA assessment of scheduled software releases." Its hotfix policy adds that they come with no warranty or promise that they will work. A system on a custom engineering hotfix needs a new one from the company's support team. BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes is fixed in BNK-2.4.2-EHF1, BNK-2.3.4-EHF1 and BNK-2.2.5-EHF1, for versions 2.4.0 to 2.4.2, 2.3.0 to 2.3.4 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.5. BIG-IP CNF, on the same version ranges, is fixed in CNF-2.4.2-EHF1, CNF-2.3.4-EHF1 and CNF-2.2.5-EHF1 for CVE-2026-121805 and CVE-2026-120285. The company checks only versions that are still within technical support, so an older release missing from its tables has not been shown to be safe. Today's flaws differ from CVE-2026-94127, an APM flaw that F5 disclosed on September 22 and that was later exploited. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day. That flaw is a heap-based buffer overflow in APM setups that serve as OAuth authorization servers, allowing attackers to run code without logging in. Today's six are stack-based overflows that need different settings. Six Other BIG-IP and BIG-IQ Flaws Today's advisories also cover six lower-rated flaws in BIG-IP and BIG-IQ, each with its own fix. The scores below are CVSS v3.1: - CVE-2026-125274 (iControl SOAP, 8.8): A user with network access and at least the Guest role can send an unauthorized management request. The company says this may allow them to run system commands, create or delete files, or disable services. It is fixed in BIG-IP 21.1.0.3, 17.5.1.10 and 17.1.3.6, and in BIG-IQ 8.4.2.3. Until then, the SOAP advisory explains how to limit iControl SOAP access to trusted networks and warns that blocking it on self-IP addresses may break high-availability setups. - CVE-2026-120718 (iControl REST, 8.1): iControl REST tokens may not expire as expected. An attacker who already holds a token may be able to extend how long it stays valid unless its owner deletes it. It is fixed in BIG-IP 21.1.0.2, 17.5.1.10, and 17.1.3.6. As a workaround, scripts that create tokens can be changed to delete them when they are no longer needed. - CVE-2026-125272 (APM, 7.5): When an APM access profile on a virtual server has a per-request policy with a form-based Logon Page, an attacker can crash TMM without logging in. It is fixed in the same engineering hotfixes as the six critical flaws. - CVE-2026-126822 (APM SAML, 7.5): When an access profile is set up as a SAML Service Provider (SP), an attacker can crash TMM without logging in. It is fixed in the same engineering hotfixes. Until then, the company suggests removing the SAML Auth agent if SAML SP is not needed, and limiting access to that virtual server to trusted client networks. - CVE-2026-126336 (APM SAML, 7.5): A SAML SP agent with encrypted assertions turned on lets an attacker crash TMM without logging in. It is fixed in BIG-IP 21.1.0.3, 17.5.1.10, and 17.1.3.6, and the company recommends a high-availability setup to reduce the impact. - CVE-2026-121812 (APM and SSL Orchestrator, 7.5): A per-request policy with the tmm.access.policytrace database key turned on lets an attacker crash TMM. The key is off by default. APM is fixed in the same engineering hotfixes, and for SSL Orchestrator the advisory lists fixes on the 21.1 and 17.1 branches only.
history.summary: Six critical vulnerabilities in F5 BIG-IP allow an attacker to crash the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) without logging in, disrupting traffic until restart, and may allow remote code execution. Each flaw requires a specific virtual server setup: an iRule using a particular command or an APM policy with certain agents, affecting modules like DNS, PEM, APM, and BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes/CNF. F5 has released engineering hotfixes as the only fix, with no workaround available, and the hotfixes come with no warranty or promise of full QA validation.

history.title: Attackers Compromise Microsoft's Agent Framework PyPI Package to Steal Cloud Credentials
history.text: Threat actors have compromised Microsoft's agent-framework package to push a credential stealer, according to reports from Aikido, Chainguard, Endor Labs, OX Security, SafeDep, Socket, StepSecurity, and Google-owned Wiz. The malicious versions, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, were published 33 minutes apart on November 17, 2026, and are designed to run a credential stealer on every Python start. As of writing, both the release versions have been quarantined on the Python Package Index (PyPI) repository. It's unclear how the attacker managed to obtain publishing access. Agent-framework is the meta-package for Microsoft Agent Framework, an open-source framework for building and orchestrating artificial intelligence (AI) agents using Python. "Both versions install Python startup hooks that silently collect credentials, environment data, and cloud identity tokens, then exfiltrate them to a webhook[.]site endpoint," Socket said in a report. Once either of the versions is installed, the package drops a .pth file in the site-packages root directory, which then gets executed automatically on every interpreter start, causing the credential stealer to run whenever Python is started in an environment, even if the package is not explicitly imported. "Each wheel adds a .pth file to site-packages," Endor Labs said. "Python executes import lines in .pth files on every interpreter start, so the stealer runs on any Python launch in an affected environment, including pip itself, whether or not anything imports Agent Framework." The names of the .pth files are below - - agent_framework_meta.pth in version 1.26.1 - af_runtime_diag.pth in version 1.26.2 The "agent_framework_meta.pth" file contains a single import statement referencing "agent_framework_meta," which then launches the stealer payload. It's capable of capturing the following data - - Environment variables based on substring-based matching - Credential files associated with Azure CLI (~/.azure/*.json), .npmrc, pip.conf, .netrc, .git-credentials, .docker/config.json, Hugging Face, Microsoft Azure DevOps agents, and .env and JSON files - Azure DevOps OIDC tokens - Azure managed-identity tokens - Azure instance metadata and retains up to 8,000 characters of the response "Besides reading credentials already on disk, the code asks the platform to issue new ones," SafeDep said. "Rotating stored secrets does not cover those." "In an Azure DevOps pipeline, SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN and SYSTEM_OIDCREQUESTURI are enough to request a federated token for api://AzureADTokenExchange. On Azure compute, it asks the managed identity endpoint for an access token to each of these resources. It uses IDENTITY_ENDPOINT or MSI_ENDPOINT on App Service and Functions, and 169.254.169[.]254 elsewhere. It also pulls instance metadata." It's worth noting that the Azure instance metadata service (IMDS) is a RESTful web service that runs on a local IP address ("169.254.169[.]254"), and provides information about the virtual machine, its region, tags, and the identity token. All the collected information is saved into a JSON document, zlib-compressed, Base64-encoded, and sent via an HTTPS POST request to a hard-coded URL ("webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb"). Version 1.26.2, on the other hand, imports a new top-level module, af_runtime_diag.py, collects GitHub Actions OIDC tokens, and expands the search patterns used for harvesting credential-related environment variables. Given that the package attracts about 190,000 downloads a month, users are advised to perform the following steps - - Isolate affected hosts and runners - Pin the package to the most recent safe version (1.26.0) and restore from a clean environment - Check for exposure to the malicious versions between 8:35 and roughly 9:20 p.m. UTC on November 17, 2026 - Search proxy and DNS logs for requests to webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb - Rotate exposed credentials from a clean system - Audit Azure identities and review sign-in and activity logs - Audit GitHub Actions workflows that deploy to Azure "The malicious agent-framework shows how attackers are targeting the AI developer ecosystem and the CI pipelines behind it," OX Security said. "While directly targeting an official Microsoft package, it seems that attackers found a way to hijack the wheel creation flow to add malicious logic inside." Agent-framework is the second Microsoft-related PyPI package to be compromised this year. In May 2026, the threat actors behind TeamPCP pushed three malicious versions of durabletask, Microsoft's Python client for the Durable Task workflow execution framework, to distribute the Mini Shai-Hulud worm.
history.summary: Threat actors compromised Microsoft's agent-framework PyPI package, releasing malicious versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 that install Python startup hooks to silently steal credentials, environment data, and cloud identity tokens. The malicious .pth files exfiltrate collected data zlib-compressed and Base64-encoded to a webhook.site endpoint, affecting environments even without explicit package import. As of November 17, 2026, both malicious versions were quarantined on PyPI, and users are advised to pin to version 1.26.0, rotate exposed credentials, and audit Azure and GitHub Actions identities.

history.title: Data breach impacts 40 Irish credit unions in reported IT provider hack
history.text: A reported cyberattack on Wellington IT has exposed sensitive information belonging to members of 50 credit unions, the majority of which are located in Ireland. Wellington IT is a Belfast-based supplier whose services are used by about 50 credit unions, including 43 in Ireland. While the company has not publicly disclosed a security incident, Minister of State Robert Troy confirmed to RTÉ that Wellington IT is the third-party service provider linked to the cybersecurity incident involving credit unions, resulting in the exposure of data from about 40 credit unions in Ireland. The company reportedly notified affected organizations of a data breach that posed a risk of financial fraud, impersonation, and targeted phishing to their members. According to the Irish Examiner, which saw the notices, Wellington IT informed customers that an automated script made five million requests to exploit an authorization flaw in the company's infrastructure. The attack unfolded between October 2 and 4, 2026, and the attacker accessed private records using valid credentials. However, the firm said it lacked activity logs that would specify which member data was compromised and therefore cannot verify the impact on individual payees. Minister R. Troy characterized the massive delay in Wellington IT notifying the credit unions as "not acceptable." At this time, the total number of impacted individuals is unknown. Sensitive information exposed At least six credit unions have independently disclosed impact linked to the incident, including Capital Credit Union, Phoenix Credit Union, St. Canice's Credit Union, First South Credit Union, Malahide Credit Union, and Limerick & District Credit Union. The announcements confirmed unauthorized access to payee information, with some noting that members' login credentials and funds haven't been affected, while others are working to determine exactly what was exposed. The notices list the following payee records saved in online banking platforms as potentially exposed: - Payee name or name associated with the payee's bank account - Nickname the member used to save the payee, if provided - International Bank Account Number (IBAN) - Bank Identifier Code (BIC) - Bank account number - Bank sort code - Payee address information - Payment reference information entered for the saved payee The records could also reveal which credit union member saved a particular payee. Account passwords, PINs, payment card details, and online banking credentials were unaffected, but union members are advised to remain vigilant for phishing and impersonation attempts. BleepingComputer has contacted Wellington IT to learn more about the incident, and we will update this post with their response once we receive it. history.summary: A cyberattack on Wellington IT exposed sensitive payee data from about 40 Irish credit unions between October 2 and 4, 2026, after an attacker exploited an authorization flaw using valid credentials and an automated script making five million requests. The company confirmed the breach posed risks of financial fraud, impersonation, and targeted phishing, but lacked activity logs to specify which member records were compromised, and at least six credit unions independently verified unauthorized access to payee information such as names, IBANs, and bank details. history.title: From Deepfakes to Helpdesk Impersonation: Why Stronger Verification Matters
history.text: In 2024, an employee at engineering firm Arup was tricked into transferring $25 million after attending a fake video conference featuring deepfake versions of their colleagues. A year later, Marks & Spencer (M&S) suffered a major cyberattack after attackers used social engineering to gain access through a third-party helpdesk. More recently, attackers have impersonated IT support staff to convince employees to hand over remote access to their devices. While the tactics differ, these incidents raise an important question for IT and security teams: how can organizations be confident that someone requesting access or authorizing a sensitive action is who they claim to be? We examine these attacks and explore how stronger identity verification and more secure workflows can help organizations defend against similar threats. The Arup Deepfake Fraud A finance employee at engineering firm Arup's Hong Kong office received an email in January 2024 that appeared to come from the company's UK-based CFO, requesting a series of transactions. Initially suspicious, the employee was convinced the request was genuine after joining a video conference featuring what appeared to be the CFO and several colleagues. However, the meeting was a deepfake. According to Hong Kong police, the attackers had used publicly available video and audio to create a convincing pre-recorded conference. The employee subsequently made multiple transfers, losing approximately HK$200 million (US$25.6 million). The M&S Cyberattack In April 2025, British retailer Marks & Spencer (M&S) suffered a major cyberattack that disrupted operations for weeks. Online orders were suspended, contactless payments and Click & Collect services were affected, and customer data was stolen. M&S initially estimated the incident would reduce its 2025/26 operating profit by around £300 million before mitigation. The attack was linked to the Scattered Spider cybercriminal group, known for using social engineering to gain access to corporate networks. M&S later confirmed that attackers had gained entry by deceiving employees at a third-party contractor, rather than exploiting a technical vulnerability in its systems. Fake IT Support Microsoft recently reported a cyberattack campaign in which threat actors impersonated IT support staff through Microsoft Teams, tricking employees into handing over remote access to their devices. The attackers contacted employees through external Teams messages or calls, posing as internal IT personnel. Using convincing pretexts such as urgent technical issues, they persuaded employees to grant remote control through screen sharing or legitimate support tools like Quick Assist. Once connected, the attackers used PowerShell to install malicious software, establish persistent access and gather information about the compromised network. Microsoft also observed attempts to move laterally towards critical infrastructure, including domain controllers and certificate authorities. The Common Thread: Trust Replacing Verification Impersonation Exploits Familiar Trust Signals Social engineering has long been a key technique in attackers’ arsenals. They don't need sophisticated malware or technical exploits to compromise an organization if they can convince someone that they're a trusted colleague. Deepfake technology makes this particularly concerning, as familiar faces and voices can be recreated. But even without AI, attackers can use convincing pretexts and trusted communication platforms to make fraudulent requests appear legitimate. Trusted Processes Can Become Attack Vectors Password resets and remote IT support are routine activities, but they can also give attackers opportunities to gain access if requests aren't properly verified. Third-party providers expand the potential attack surface; organizations may have strong controls over their own systems but less visibility into how external support teams verify identities and authorize sensitive actions. Employees Can't Be Expected to Spot Every Impersonation Attempt Security awareness training helps employees recognize suspicious requests, but even well-trained staff can be deceived by convincing impersonation attempts. Attackers will carry out reconnaissance beforehand to gather information that makes their social engineering attempts appear like routine requests. Organizations need reliable verification processes that support employees when they're asked to make security-sensitive decisions, rather than leaving them to judge whether someone can be trusted. How Can Organizations Mitigate These Risks? Independently Verify Sensitive Requests For financial transactions, privileged access, and other sensitive requests, organizations should require independent confirmation through trusted channels. This might include contacting the requester using previously verified details or introducing additional authentication into approval workflows. Verify IT Support Requests Before Granting Access Where support processes are managed through internal applications or automated workflows, additional identity verification can help ensure that sensitive requests are made by authorized users. These measures should be supported by broader security controls like phishing-resistant MFA and least-privilege access, while monitoring for suspicious account activity. Make Strong Verification Part of Everyday Security As social engineering tactics become more convincing, organizations can't rely on employees recognizing every fraudulent request. history.title: Russian APT Poses as Employee of Hacked Firm to Breach Another US Organization
history.text: Russia-linked APT Star Blizzard hacked a US organization by impersonating an employee at another US organization it had previously compromised, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) reports. Also tracked as Callisto, Cold Relic, Cold River, UNC4057, and Gossamer Bear, and active for over a decade, Star Blizzard has been formally associated by the US with Russia’s intelligence service FSB. The APT is known for mounting sophisticated phishing and malware campaigns to collect information relevant to the Russian government, and to use victims’ data in attacks on subsequent targets. Star Blizzard “has been highly successful at compromising high-value targets (including government officials, defense contractors, and non-governmental organizations (NGOs) across Europe and North America) while maintaining a consistent operational tempo,” Google says. In a recent attack against a US organization, Star Blizzard impersonated an employee of another organization it had breached months earlier. Google, which tracks the group as Cold Relic, believes the hackers likely used contact and relationship information obtained during the earlier intrusion to select and deceive their new target. The first organization was hit in late 2025, using the compromised credentials of a super admin account. The APT leveraged a residential proxy network close to the victim and relied on multi-factor authentication (MFA) push notification fatigue to register a device to the victim’s tenant. Next, the group downloaded the organization’s entire cloud storage drive, accessed the admin console to fingerprint defenses and remove evidence of the initial intrusion, exported full employee lists, and launched a domain-wide export. According to Google, the group used passkeys, rogue MFA devices, and MFA backup codes to maintain persistent access to the victim organization for several months. It also exfiltrated emails and targeted cloud drive documents containing information of interest. “When the threat actor was removed from the victim organization’s infrastructure, GTIG observed Cold Relic leveraging email accounts impersonating employees of the victim organization. These impersonated accounts were used to target both internal employees and associates within the same professional circles with renewed social engineering attempts,” Google says. The APT impersonated an employee at the victim organization to establish communication with the second victim organization via a secure messaging application. Ultimately, it shared phishing links designed to steal credentials and Entra ID authentication tokens, and used the secrets to register a new MFA device to the second organization’s SSO solution to retain access to the compromised account. “By impersonating someone known in the same professional circles as the new target, Cold Relic increased their chance of phishing success. Ultimately, in this case, Cold Relic was able to obtain credentials to the organization and perform bulk download of files accessible in the compromised user’s cloud drive,” Google says. To maintain persistence, the APT registered rogue MFA devices, passkeys, and MFA backup codes, conducted aggressive data collection and exfiltration, and searched for credentials, employee information, email archives, documents, and any other information it could use in subsequent spear-phishing attacks. The threat actor also changed its profile name in the secure messaging application used in this intrusion, likely to reuse it in another attack. “Cold Relic’s campaigns demonstrate the convergence of human-centric social engineering and cloud identity abuse. By obtaining access to strategic personnel rosters and operational documents, Russian intelligence services turn legitimate business communications into attack vectors against trusted partners,” Google notes. history.title: Last of Five Defendants Sentenced in US Scattered Spider Hacking Case
history.text: A British Scattered Spider hacker will spend six years in a US federal prison for his part in a conspiracy to hack companies and take at least $11.6 million in cryptocurrency from individuals across the US. Tyler Robert Buchanan, 24, from Dundee, Scotland, was arrested in Spain in May 2024 and has been held by US authorities since April 2025. He pleaded guilty in April 2026 to conspiracy to commit wire fraud and aggravated identity theft. Between September 2021 and April 2023, the Scattered Spider group texted hundreds of phishing lures to staff at telecommunications, technology, interactive entertainment, cloud communications, and cryptocurrency companies. Links in the texts pointed to phishing websites where recipients were tricked into entering credentials and personal information. Login details captured by the cybercriminals ended up in a Telegram channel managed by Buchanan and an accomplice. With the stolen credentials, the hackers broke into employee accounts and company systems and took confidential information. That information helped them pinpoint and access cryptocurrency accounts and wallets owned by individuals. To defeat two-factor authentication, they took over victims’ phone numbers through SIM swaps, moving the numbers to devices under their control. The theft total has grown from the $8 million cited at the time of Buchanan’s plea. The court will hold a restitution hearing on December 11. Buchanan is the final defendant in the five-person case to receive a sentence. Ahmed Hossam Eldin Elbadawy and Evans Onyeaka Osiebo, both of Texas, were each given 45 months in September and August, respectively. Noah Michael Urban is serving 10 years in federal prison, while Joel Martin Evans received a two-year term. Earlier this year, two other Scattered Spider members, Thalha Jubair and Owen Flowers, were sentenced to jail in the United Kingdom for a cyberattack targeting Transport for London (TfL). history.title: Drupal Patches Critical Installer Flaw That Could Give Unauthenticated Attackers Control of Sites
history.text: Under specific conditions, a critical vulnerability in Drupal core can allow an attacker without login credentials to use the built-in installer to attempt to reinstall a site. That can lead to a site takeover or remote code execution, and the project rates the vulnerable configurations as uncommon. Fixed releases for all supported branches shipped yesterday. The Drupal Security Team disclosed the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-132165, yesterday and rated it critical, 18 out of 25 on the project's risk scale. The installer ships in every copy of Drupal core as the file /core/install.php and stays on the site after installation. Core's default .htaccess rules do not block requests to it, so blocking it is left to each site. No attacks are reported in the security advisory, which rates exploitation as complex and records an existing proof-of-concept exploit. Some exploit paths are blocked where the web server cannot write to or change permissions on settings.php. The team had told site owners in an advance notice earlier this week to set aside time for the update, warning that exploits may be developed within hours or days. Every release below 10.6.22 is affected, along with Drupal 11 releases from 11.0.0 before 11.3.22 and from 11.4.0 before 11.4.13. What to Do Now The fixed versions, detailed in the project's release notes, are: - Drupal 11.4.x: update to 11.4.13 - Drupal 11.3.x: update to 11.3.22 - Drupal 10.6.x: update to 10.6.22 The team recommends blocking the installer even after updating. Sites that cannot update yet should follow the project's installer guidance, updated yesterday, which describes three options: a deny rule in the web server configuration, an .htaccess rule, or removing the file and keeping it removed with Composer scripts. Sites that use the Drupal Steward protection service are already protected from known attack vectors, according to the team, and should still update in case new vectors emerge. Drupal 11.2.x and earlier, 10.5.x and earlier, and Drupal 8 and 9 are end-of-life and get no fix. The 11.3.x branch and Drupal 10 lose security coverage altogether in December under the project's support schedule. In the week of November 8, 154,485 of the 528,430 sites reporting usage data to drupal.org, about 29 percent, were running end-of-life branches. The flaw was found by Anthropic's OSS Scanner, an automated service the AI company launched on October 8 to look for vulnerabilities in open-source projects that opt in. Findings go to maintainers without human review, each with a reproducer and, where available, a candidate patch, according to its launch announcement. Drupal's security team said on November 2 that a surge of security reports, which it attributes to AI tools, is more than it can sustain at its current funding, and that it is cutting security coverage for core minor versions from 12 months to 8 starting in 2027. This is the second critical remote code execution flaw fixed in Drupal core in two months, after the Field UI flaw patched on October 14, which also had at least one exploit path that needed no login.
history.summary: A critical vulnerability (CVE-2026-132165) in Drupal core allows unauthenticated attackers to exploit the built-in installer under specific conditions, potentially leading to site takeover or remote code execution. Fixed versions have been released: Drupal 10.6.22, 11.3.22, and 11.4.13, with exploitation rated as complex and an existing proof-of-concept exploit noted. Fix: Update to the fixed Drupal versions and block or remove the /core/install.php installer file using web server configuration, .htaccess rules, or Composer scripts.

history.title: Critical VMware vCenter Flaw (CVSS 9.8) Lets Network Attackers Bypass Authentication
history.text: A critical flaw in VMware vCenter lets an attacker with network access bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system, Broadcom, which owns VMware, said in an advisory published today. Fixed versions are out for all supported branches, and the company lists no workaround. vCenter is the central console for managing an organization's ESX hosts and virtual machines. The vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2026-123890 and is rated 9.8 on the CVSS scoring system. "VMware vCenter contains an authentication bypass vulnerability in the VMware Directory Service," the advisory says. In an FAQ published with the advisory, the company says the issue "qualifies under ITIL methodologies as an emergency change," and urges organizations to consult their security staff immediately on timing. The company has not reported any attacks exploiting the flaw, or any public exploit code. It also does not say what level of access an attacker gains after the bypass. Credit for reporting the bug goes to Google-owned Mandiant. The bug is present in vCenter 8.0, 9.0, and 9.1, and in the vCenter builds that ship inside VMware Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, and the Telco Cloud Platform and Telco Cloud Infrastructure products. That includes the older Cloud Foundation 5.x line. It is there whether or not Enhanced Linked Mode is in use. Older versions are not cleared. The company no longer evaluates versions past end of support, and says vSphere 6.5 and 6.7 should be presumed affected. The same goes for vSphere 7.0, which left general support in October 2025, and whose customers can request a patch under an extended support contract. None of the five flaws in the advisory lets code run on an ESX host from inside a virtual machine, and ESX itself is not affected, the advisory FAQ says. There is no fallback for systems that cannot be updated yet: asked whether a workaround exists, the FAQ answers "Not as listed by Broadcom," while noting that mitigations may still exist in an organization's own defenses. The updates are cumulative and cannot be installed through vCenter Quick Patch. Virtual machines continue running while vCenter installs the update, though management access drops briefly, and some encryption operations against a Standard Key Provider become unavailable until vCenter is back online. One warning applies to upgrades already in progress: installing vCenter 8.0 U3m or 9.0.2.0200 blocks a later upgrade to VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.1, a conflict the FAQ calls a "Back-in-Time" issue. The options are to upgrade vCenter to 9.1.1 first and apply the security update there, or to wait briefly for VCF 9.1.2. The bypass is the second critical authentication flaw in the VMware Directory Service this year. The earlier vCenter flaws, patched on July 29, included CVE-2026-59309, another 9.8-rated bypass in the same component per the July advisory, alongside a directory-traversal bug, CVE-2026-59310. Attacks on that traversal flaw began five days after its disclosure, German incident response firm QUIRSO assessed in August, linking them with moderate confidence to a suspected China-nexus actor. The August attacks compromised an estimated 361 IP addresses in 47 countries and deployed Babuk-derived ransomware on ESXi hosts. Broadcom has reported no attacks on the new bypass. The advisory also fixes four lower-severity flaws, rated 6.7 to 8.1: a SQL injection (CVE-2026-123891) and a command injection (CVE-2026-123892) in SDDC Manager, a privilege escalation to root on the SDDC Manager appliance (CVE-2026-123893), and a SAML token signature bypass in VMware Tools for Windows (CVE-2026-123894), exploitable only where Guest Alias mapping is configured. Each needs an authenticated or already privileged actor, and the last one stays inside the guest virtual machine.
history.summary: Critical VMware vCenter flaw CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS 9.8) lets network attackers bypass authentication in the VMware Directory Service. Broadcom has released fixed versions for all supported branches and states no workaround exists. The vulnerability affects vCenter 8.0, 9.0, 9.1 and related platforms including older Cloud Foundation builds, with no reported exploits or public code in the wild. Fix: Broadcom has released cumulative security updates for all supported vCenter branches; systems should be updated immediately as no workaround is available.

history.title: CISA Warns of 4 Exploited Flaws Linked to Ransomware, Cryptomining, and LLMjacking Attacks
history.text: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Wednesday added four vulnerabilities impacting Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM), BerriAI LiteLLM, Apache Axis, and Vanderbilt University Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation. The vulnerabilities are listed below - - CVE-2026-90436 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An unsafe reflection vulnerability in Apache Axis that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code. - CVE-2026-90817 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A code injection vulnerability in REDCap that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the server. - CVE-2026-40217 (CVSS score: 8.8) - An unprotected alternate channel vulnerability in LiteLLM that could allow a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code via bytecode rewriting at the /guardrails/test_custom_code URI. - CVE-2024-10441 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An improper encoding or escaping of output vulnerability in Synology DSM that could allow a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code via unspecified vectors. "An attacker could exploit this via crafted HTTP requests that access an unintended controller route from a public survey context and supply a crafted file-path or stream parameter during data import processing," CISA said about CVE-2026-90817. "Exploitation requires knowledge of a valid public survey hash." The addition of CVE-2026-90436 to the KEV catalog follows reports that the flaw is exploited in conjunction with the 4EverAble2Shell vulnerabilities affecting N-able N-central to deploy cryptocurrency miners on vulnerable servers. Rapid7, in its own analysis of the flaw, said it detected exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 against Atlassian Confluence Data Center in a customer environment by taking advantage of the fact that the corporate workspace platform uses the Axis library as part of its XML-RPC and SOAP APIs. "To be vulnerable, the Confluence instance must have the 'Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP)' enabled," Atlassian said. "Please note that this setting was turned off by default for new installations starting in Confluence 3.0. This feature was fully removed in Confluence 10.0." In the activity documented by Rapid7, threat actors are said to have weaponized the flaw to run shell commands and scripts fetched from temporary Pinggy and Cloudflare Tunnel domains, followed by enumerating the compromised environment. The incident was flagged on November 13, 2026. "Just over three minutes after the first observed execution, the attackers were authenticating to MySQL with Confluence's own database credentials, querying page bodies, application links, and attachments with names associated with credentials, tokens, VPN configurations, and private keys," Rapid7 said. "The attacker's scripts, likely AI-generated, then targeted files in Confluence's default location for uploaded page attachments (/var/atlassian/application-data/confluence/attachments/v4/), parsed Office documents, searched for credentials, and hunted for payment card numbers, using Luhn checks to filter out false positives." In addition, the attackers have been found to map various internal services, use a Confluence application credential to query the internal Atlassian Crowd API for users and group memberships, and attempt to carry out a Kerberos-based credential harvesting technique called AS-REP Roasting. Although these efforts were unsuccessful, the threat actor managed to acquire a service account credential and queried a production cloud data warehouse. About 12 hours after the first exploit request, the attacker signed in to Microsoft 365 as an integration service account using legacy authentication from "192.238.253[.]176." CVE-2026-90436, which affects Axis 1.x versions, remains unpatched as Axis 1 has reached end-of-life (EoL) status. It's recommended to migrate to a different SOAP engine, such as Apache Axis 2/Java. Alternatively, users can use a build of Axis with the patch from a July 12, 2026, commit applied. As for CVE-2026-90817, Safe Security said in a report published late last month that it observed an unknown threat abusing the flaw to "stage a transient web shell, followed by an in-memory loader that retrieved XMRig disguised as image files, masqueraded the miner as syslog-ng, and established persistence through cron and an added SSH key." The exploitation of CVE-2026-40217 stems from a Google Threat Intelligence Group report this week in which threat actors have leveraged the vulnerability to elevate limited-access inference keys into full administrative credentials and establish persistence as part of LLMjacking attacks aimed at financial services, retail, transportation, and technology organizations in North America, South America, and the Asia Pacific region. Rounding off the list is CVE-2024-10441, which Synology disclosed earlier this month as being exploited in ransomware attacks targeting Network Attached Storage (NAS) devices. The attacks have been found to result in the deployment of C3RB3R ransomware. In light of active exploitation, federal agencies have been recommended to apply fixes or necessary mitigations for DSM, REDCap, and Axis flaws by November 21, 2026, and for the LiteLLM flaw by December 2, 2026.
history.summary: CISA added four vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, citing active exploitation linked to ransomware, cryptomining, and LLMjacking attacks. CVE-2026-90436 in Apache Axis allows unauthenticated remote code execution and has been exploited to deploy cryptocurrency miners, though the flaw remains unpatched as Axis 1.x is end-of-life, with migration to Axis 2 or applying a July 2026 commit recommended. CVE-2026-90817 in REDCap and CVE-2026-40217 in LiteLLM were also added due to evidence of exploitation for arbitrary code execution and LLMjacking campaigns targeting financial, retail, and technology organizations. CVE-2024-10441 in Synology DSM was exploited in ransomware attacks deploying C3RB3R ransomware, with federal agencies advised to apply mitigations by November 21, 2026 for DSM, REDCap, and Axis flaws, and by December 2, 2026 for the LiteLLM flaw.

history.title: Everything Is a Web Application, Including Your Firewall
history.text: One of the early targets of PHP2Shell exploitation was the firewall. On October 28, Palo Alto Networks confirmed that attackers were exploiting the two PHP vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, against PAN-OS management interfaces exposed to the internet. Both flaws let anyone execute code on the web server without authentication. The disclosure itself went a little wrong. Details leaked on October 20, ahead of the coordinated release, and the PHP project shipped an emergency patch the next day. The vulnerabilities require no authentication, but they are not easy to exploit reliably. It takes skill and additional knowledge about the target system. Where it matters a lot is appliances, which run identical, often outdated software that an attacker can study in advance. That is the bigger picture. An awful lot of web applications control critical devices in your network. Almost anything is a web application to some extent. That often goes unrecognized, and as a result those applications aren't adequately protected. Everything is a web application. That is the motto of the SANS course I teach, SEC522: Application Security: Securing Web Applications, APIs, and Microservices. Web application security has traditionally been treated as a developer issue, yet anyone protecting a network must understand how web applications work to properly defend them. Why Appliances Are the Softer Target On ordinary web servers, address space layout randomization (ASLR) is one of the features that makes exploitation harder. It shuffles where code and data sit in memory, so an exploit can't rely on fixed addresses. VulnCheck's early analysis found the bugs exploitable on ARM64 systems and on x86 systems without ASLR. Few public exploits bypassed ASLR on x86-64, and the one VulnCheck confirmed worked only against a single PHP build. VulnCheck's own exploit chained a memory leak to get code execution with ASLR enabled. Appliances change that math, not because the protections are missing, but because every device on a given software version runs the same binaries, so an attacker can work out memory offsets in advance. The PAN-OS exploit still had to defeat ASLR, leaking the libphp.so base address through the Set-Cookie header, and SELinux confined the resulting shell. PAN-OS also ships end-of-life PHP versions (8.0.30 and 7.4.33). Israeli security firm Dream, working with Palo Alto Networks on the investigation, found the attacker had obtained PAN-OS firmware, decrypted it, extracted the PHP libraries, and built precise memory profiles for nine software versions. The actor then chained PHP2Shell with a Linux kernel flaw (Fragnesia, CVE-2026-46300) to gain root on 25 systems (24 firewalls and one management server) in the U.S., Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. Web application security tends to focus on large, cloud-based applications. It's often the little things, the mosquitoes on the internet, that do you in. Appliances run predictable, often outdated software, and they are everywhere. HTTP Is More Complex Than Your Defenses Assume HTTP is a very complex protocol with lots of options. To upload a file, a client doesn't have to send it in one piece. It can send the body in chunks without declaring its total length, and, if the server decompresses request bodies, compress it, which makes it difficult for a web server to calculate how much memory it needs to store it. Memory-safety bugs remain common as a result, in web applications and in the web servers running them. In PHP2Shell, a crafted multipart upload pushes PHP past its memory limit while it is still parsing the request, before any application code runs. The bugs are in what PHP leaves behind when it aborts the request: uninitialized request memory (CVE-2026-109618) and a pointer to freed memory (CVE-2026-109619). The request doesn't need to be large, either. Deeply nested, empty file fields make PHP allocate far more memory than the body contains, so a request well under the default 8 MB post_max_size can still exhaust the default 128 MB memory limit. Defenders must understand the protocol to know what these vulnerabilities look like, for example to write signatures that detect the exploits. The same complexity limits the middle boxes we rely on. They can even interfere in ways nobody planned. Intruder found that nginx in front of PAN-OS buffered chunked request bodies, which broke public exploit chains. Web application firewalls are often not adequate, and file uploads are key functionality for a lot of web applications, so blocking them outright isn't an option. That takes out many of the traditional defenses. What remains is knowing where your critical web applications are. Identify them, starting with the admin interfaces on your firewalls and other network equipment, and restrict access to them. Palo Alto's own guidance for PHP2Shell was to remove internet access to management interfaces and limit them to trusted internal IP addresses. If you rely on a web application firewall, configure it properly and understand how much protection it does and doesn't provide. Risk Was the Hardest Call The clearest lesson from PHP2Shell is how difficult it can be to accurately determine the risk from a vulnerability like this. Prioritization is always a big issue for defenders, particularly with today's flood of vulnerabilities, and this one was hard to read from every angle. The scores told different stories. The PHP project rated both flaws 9.2 under CVSS 4.0, and Fortinet's PSIRT listed 9.8 under CVSS v3. Palo Alto initially scored the issue 8.7 for its own products and listed it at moderate urgency, raised it to 9.2 Critical with the highest urgency on October 27, and confirmed exploitation a week after its advisory went out. Many public proofs of concept didn't work, so a flood of attempts in your logs said little about whether a given server was at risk. We are adding these lessons to SEC522: how to assess risk, how protections like ASLR reduce it, and why appliances remain softer targets. history.title: Hackers Exploit Cisco Expressway Vulnerability Soon After PoC Release
history.text: Hackers exploited a critical Cisco Expressway vulnerability to breach a Russian organization soon after proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit code was released publicly, according to cybersecurity firm F6. Expressway gateways allow remote employees, partners, and third-party users to securely connect to an organization’s collaboration services, including video calls, voice calls, and instant messaging. Tracked as CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score of 9.8), the flaw can be exploited without authentication by remote attackers with network access to a device, allowing them to execute commands as root. It affects virtual and appliance versions of Expressway Core and Expressway Edge, but only when the devices are clustered. Cisco, which disclosed the issue on October 21, said it resides in the Expressway database service feature and stems from persistent cookies. An attacker possessing the persistent cookies could reach the database service and issue certain remote procedure call (RPC) commands, gaining the ability to run root-level commands on the underlying operating system. Expressway X15.5.20 resolves the vulnerability. There are no workarounds, and customers on X14 or earlier releases need to move to a fixed release, Cisco says. The advisory has not been revised since its initial release and still states that Cisco is unaware of public announcements or malicious use of the flaw. However, a PoC exploit has since been posted on GitHub, and F6 says the attack it investigated came shortly after. According to F6, the attackers first breached two Expressway X15.5.3 devices exposed to the internet. They then pivoted from one of them to two other cluster nodes sitting on the organization’s internal network. After securing root privileges, the attackers prepared tools for lateral movement. These included custom Python scripts designed to scan the network, locate SMB resources, interact with SQL Server and WinRM, and search GitLab repositories, aiming to exfiltrate credentials and other sensitive information. F6 determined that the attackers modified the scripts on the fly, during the attack. “The source code contained characteristic comments and descriptions of fixes indicating the use of an AI assistant,” the company says. F6 did not name the victim or attribute the attack to a known threat actor. To detect exploitation, F6 points to the Erlang system log on Expressway devices. The security firm has also published IP addresses and file paths associated with the attack in a Russian-language press release. Although Cisco lists no workarounds, F6 recommends that organizations unable to patch immediately block connections to TCP ports 4371–4372 at the firewall, except from the IP addresses of trusted cluster nodes. SecurityWeek has reached out to Cisco for comment on F6’s findings and will update this article if the company responds. history.title: Critical NGINX ‘NGINX2Root’ bugs let attackers hijack servers
history.text: Two critical NGINX vulnerabilities dubbed "nginx2root" allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code remotely on vulnerable web servers, with researchers demonstrating how the flaws can be chained with a Linux kernel bug to gain root access. The two HTTP/2 vulnerabilities were discovered independently by researchers at Xint, Wiz, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, and Rapid7, while Xint also discovered three additional NGINX RCE flaws. Censys later reproduced the underlying memory corruption conditions in four of the five flaws through lab testing, but did not achieve remote code execution. The first of the two "nginx2root" flaws is CVE-2026-123007, a flow-control bug that can corrupt memory in an NGINX worker. It impacts all versions from 1.31.8 down to 1.9.5, released in 2015. Wiz demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution on a server hosting ordinary static files over HTTP/2 with TLS, while Xint demoed root access by chaining it with a separate Linux kernel flaw. Xint says the separate vulnerability affects the Linux kernel's SCTP subsystem and can be used to escape an NGINX Docker container and gain root privileges on the underlying host. The second flaw is CVE-2026-123633, a use-after-free problem that affects NGINX when it accepts HTTP/2 connections and proxies requests to a backend. It impacts all versions from 1.19.7 through 1.31.8. When the worker runs low on connection slots, it can close an active connection and free memory that a request still uses. Wiz also demonstrated remote code execution via CVE-2026-123633, but the firm is not publicly releasing its proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits at this time. The other three flaws the researchers discovered and F5 fixed are CVE-2026-121810, CVE-2026-123634, and CVE-2026-113425, all use-after-free vulnerabilities affecting HTTP/3 reverse proxying, DNS resolution with subrequests, and mail proxy authentication, respectively. The flaws were fixed in NGINX Open Source 1.30.7 stable and 1.31.9 mainline. NGINX Plus users should update to versions 37.0.8.1 or 37.3.0.1. F5’s latest security update also addresses five more vulnerabilities not highlighted in the Wiz or Xint reports. The most notable is CVE-2026-118899, a high-severity issue that allows an unauthenticated attacker to cause a worker to enter an infinite loop while reading a request body over TLS 1.3, resulting in denial of service. For system administrators, it is recommended to upgrade immediately to the latest NGINX release, or temporarily disable HTTP/2 until an upgrade is possible. However, this mitigation only covers the two "nginx2root" flaws. Evaluating the risk Regarding the real exploitability risk of "nginx2root," security researcher Florian Roth says it's worse than Node2Shell and Java2Shell, but doesn’t appear to be an imminent threat for most NGINX deployments. Commenting on X, Roth said the flaws are exploitable in non-default configurations, warning that claims of widespread exposure based solely on NGINX version numbers are misleading. Xint previously reported that 98.9% of NGINX hosts disclosing recognizable versions were running software within the affected range, but this does not account for whether HTTP/2 is enabled or security fixes have been backported. The two HTTP/2 flaws require an unpatched server with HTTP/2 enabled on a listener an attacker can reach, while CVE-2026-123633 also requires NGINX to proxy requests to a backend. Roth scanned a sample of a few hundred NGINX HTTPS endpoints from Shodan and found that roughly 66% of them support HTTP/2, but confirming actual exposure requires checking the server’s configuration and whether a fix has been backported. According to Censys' live exposure tracker, approximately 8.8 million NGINX services were potentially exposed to CVE-2026-123007 as of November 19, based on affected version numbers and HTTP/2 support. The company reports that more than 511,000 previously exposed services have already been patched or mitigated, while another 104 million NGINX services do not disclose their versions, making it difficult to determine whether they are affected.
