history.title: ThreatsDay: GPT-6.2 Jailbreak Flaws, BubbleLoader PNG Malware, $500M Ransom Demands + 17 More Stories
history.text: The easiest way to fool someone is to give them something they already expect. A job offer. A message about a service outage. A familiar app. Nothing looks strange at first. And that's the problem. This week's stories show how ordinary things are being used to steal data, spread malware, and get people to hand over access. There's another shift worth watching. AI is making some attacks easier to run and harder to spot. Stolen data can now be searched like a shopping catalog. Phishing emails can be tested and rewritten until they get through. At the same time, researchers are finding that even powerful AI systems have safety gaps of their own. And while everyone is watching the new tools, the old problems haven't gone anywhere. Third-party breaches, years of hidden spying, ransomware, and security fixes still need attention. Some stories are clever. Others are painfully simple. Here's what caught our attention this week. The threats change every week. Subscribe, and we’ll alert you when each new ThreatsDay Bulletin is out. - Faster, more secure AI coding Google has unveiled Gemini 4 Neon, its latest frontier model capable of delivering reasoning faster and more cost-efficiently. According to the company's DeepMind division, it also produces more secure code than Carbon across all easy, medium, and hard challenges on AutoBaxBench, achieving state-of-the-art on the hard tier (76%). "Neon for cyber delivers frontier-level performance across the code hardening lifecycle — vulnerability finding, validating, and patching — all while being faster and more cost-efficient than large frontier models," Google said. "Neon achieves state-of-the-art performance on SEC-bench Pro (90.5%), while costing roughly half as much per challenge." Gemini 4 Neon for cyber is rolling out to trusted defenders in the coming days as part of the Fairwind Program. - Major leap in AI cyber capabilities OpenAI has introduced GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol with a "significant jump" in cyber capabilities. "They find and exploit vulnerabilities more effectively, write more secure code, and produce better patches, with substantial token-efficiency gains on several evaluations," OpenAI said. "Like GPT‑6 Astra, 6.2 Astra and Sol meet the Critical threshold for cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework." The company also said it has made defensive capabilities a core focus by allowing the models to write secure code from the start. The development comes amid a disclosure from the U.K. AI Security Institute (AISI) that it developed a universal jailbreak against two pre-release versions of OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra in half the queries required for GPT-6 Astra, adding it identified a "substantial regression in jailbreak robustness relative to GPT-6 Astra." OpenAI has since addressed the regression. - Urgent WordPress security update WordPress has released WordPress 7.1.5 with fixes for multiple security issues. "Because this is a security release, it is recommended that you update your sites immediately," WordPress said. The patches have also been backported to all branches eligible to receive security fixes (currently through 4.7). - Independent AI safety assessments OpenAI will embed independent evaluators from Apollo Research, Goodfire, METR, and Transluce in its organization as part of a pilot to help support its safety work. The embedded assessors will focus on model alignment and monitoring, training run monitoring, post-training alignment evaluations, and assessing "whether models could covertly work against their developers’ intentions and whether our safeguards would detect such behavior." "Embedded assessments give independent experts deep access to a lab’s internal models and systems to assess model alignment and the effectiveness of safeguards over an extended period of time, especially where relevant to our safety cases," the company said. "Based on what each evaluation needs, assessors receive access to some of the same internal resources our researchers use, including model checkpoints, source code, training and evaluation data, monitoring systems, technical documentation, and discussions with the researchers and engineers responsible for the work. This access gives assessors the evidence and context to pursue independent evaluations and uncover failures we may not have anticipated." OpenAI's safety practices have been under intense scrutiny since July, when two of its models escaped containment, accessed the open internet and hacked a company called Hugging Face. The pilot, however, limits how much researchers can disclose, with OpenAI reserving the right to redact evidence or confidential information to substantiate the outcome of their evaluations. - $500 million ransomware extortion case Roman Khlynovskiy, 43, a Kazak national, has been extradited from Italy to the U.S. to face charges for his alleged role in a ransomware and extortion conspiracy that targeted U.S. schools, hospitals, and healthcare entities. "Khlynovskiy and other members of the '8-Digits Team' repeatedly targeted hospitals and schools, extorting victims and threatening to release highly sensitive information," said FBI Director Kash Patel. "This widespread extortion campaign resulted in over $500 million in ransom demands." The 8-Digits Team is said to have been affiliated with the INC and Lynx ransomware, and targeted victims in at least six states, including both schools and hospitals. Khlynovskiy was arrested in Italy in July 2025 while vacationing with his family. He is facing a maximum penalty of 27 years in prison on computer fraud, money laundering, wire fraud, extortion and identity theft charges. - AI model extraction tactics exposed An exclusive report from Reuters has revealed that Chinese entities are adopting sophisticated methods to conduct distillation attacks against American AI models and use the outputs to train domestic rivals, according to a review of more than 300 Chinese academic papers, patents, corporate disclosures, recruitment notices, and government documents. "Chinese researchers [are] using U.S. models to produce answers to questions, build computer code and find solutions to difficult problems, with Chinese companies then developing software to automate the process and specialist workers preparing material for training smaller domestic models," the report said. - AI-driven stolen data marketplace A criminal marketplace promoted on underground forums is selling data stolen from computers infected with infostealer malware, along with AI-written profiles of their owners, according to Hudson Rock. The seller has claimed registration for the service is open and free. "The reviewed listings present each computer with a description of its apparent owner, workplace, applications, and potentially valuable data," Hudson Rock said. "Buyers can search those descriptions using natural language and combine the results with filters such as country, operating system, and price. The result is a catalog in which a compromised machine can be presented as a clinic’s reception desk, a defense contractor's household computer, or a government employee's family workstation. The service is marketing the context around the stolen data as part of the product." - North Korean ransomware campaign The North Korean hacking group known as Kimsuky group has been observed distributing the Funhouse ransomware via a malicious Hangul document that was disguised as a resume. "The Funhouse ransomware was identified as a variant of previously disclosed endpoint ransomware, and the tools used in this attack — such as Quasar RAT — as well as the overall attack chain shared numerous similarities with Kimsuky’s endpoint ransomware distribution cases observed since the first half of 2026," AhnLab said. - Gemini chat retention extended Google is extending how long it keeps temporary Gemini chats and conversations made with chat history turned off to around two months, saying the change aims to improve safety and security as AI systems become more capable. The investigation was launched in January 2020. "The Download My Data tool was presented to Tinder users as a way to request a copy of their personal data," the Data Protection Commission (DPC) said. "It failed to provide users with all of their personal data. Certain categories of information were omitted without notice to the user, or provided in summary form only." history.title: CISA Adds Four Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
history.text: CISA Adds Four Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. - CVE-2025-42884 SAP NetWeaver Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in Data Query Logic Vulnerability - CVE-2026-76466 Cisco Expressway Series Use of Hard-coded Credentials Vulnerability - CVE-2026-123890 VMWare vCenter Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel Vulnerability - CVE-2026-129448 Apache Roller Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance. history.title: F5 releases emergency patches for critical BIG-IP RCE flaws
history.text: US cybersecurity company F5 warned customers to patch five BIG-IP vulnerabilities that attackers can exploit to trigger denial-of-service (DoS) or gain remote code execution. Tracked as CVE-2026-121805, CVE-2026-120292, CVE-2026-120285, CVE-2026-116953, and CVE-2026-123637, these stack-based buffer overflow flaws affect the company's BIG-IP Access Policy Manager (APM) centralized access management proxy solution and the BIG-IP iRules programmable scripting feature. All five security issues are rated critical severity, and unauthenticated threat actors can exploit them to terminate the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) and execute arbitrary code remotely on systems with vulnerable configurations. The company also released engineering hotfixes for a high-severity BIG-IP APM SAML vulnerability (CVE-2026-126822) stemming from an integer underflow (wrap or wraparound) weakness that remote, unauthenticated threat actors can abuse in denial-of-service (DoS) attacks. "Traffic is disrupted while the TMM process restarts. This vulnerability allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to cause a denial-of-service (DoS) on the BIG-IP system and may perform RCE," F5 said. "There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only." F5 said it has no mitigation measures for these flaws and advised security teams to install the out-of-band hotfixes released on Wednesday to address them on vulnerable devices. Internet threat watchdog Shadowserver currently tracks more than 177,000 BIG-IP instances and over 14,600 IP addresses with BIG-IP APM fingerprints exposed online. However, there is no information on how many are honeypots or have already been patched against these vulnerabilities. Although the company hasn't flagged any of these issues as exploited in attacks, admins should upgrade systems to the latest version as soon as possible, since cybercrime and nation-state threat groups have often abused F5 vulnerabilities in the wild. Attackers have targeted F5 security flaws to breach corporate networks, map internal servers, hijack devices, deploy data-wiping malware, and steal sensitive files from victims worldwide in recent years. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has flagged seven F5 vulnerabilities as actively exploited since November 2021, four of them also used by ransomware gangs. Most recently, in September, F5 also patched a critical BIG-IP APM vulnerability (CVE-2026-94127) that is being actively exploited in zero-day remote code execution attacks. One year ago, F5 also disclosed that state-backed hackers breached its systems in August 2025 to steal source code and information on undisclosed BIG-IP security vulnerabilities. F5 is a Fortune 500 tech company that provides cybersecurity, application delivery networking (ADN), and other services to more than 23,000 customers, including 80% of the Fortune Global 500 and 48 of Fortune 50 companies. history.title: Bell Canada says 'agentic' hacker stole enterprise customer data
history.text: Bell Canada has confirmed that an "agentic" threat actor breached its systems on November 17, 2026, and stole enterprise customer data, including information from a system used to order and provision telecommunications circuits. Bell is one of Canada's largest telecommunications providers, offering wireless, internet, television, and enterprise networking services. BleepingComputer first learned of the incident after receiving a tip from a customer who shared a breach notification sent by Bell's Information Security Team. According to the notification, an unauthorized party accessed a pre-production environment of Bell's Maximo system, which the company uses to order and provision telecommunications network connections. Bell warned that information belonging to the recipient's organization may have been stolen, including business contact information such as names, job titles, corporate email addresses, phone numbers, and business addresses. The potentially exposed data also includes information contained in ticket titles and some IP addresses associated with network elements or systems, along with limited contextual information. However, Bell said the affected dataset did not contain credentials, highly sensitive personal information, PDFs, file attachments, or other supplementary information stored in Maximo. When contacted by BleepingComputer, Bell confirmed the intrusion and said that an "agentic threat actor" had accessed multiple systems and stolen enterprise customer data. "Bell is investigating a cybersecurity incident that occurred on November 17 in which an agentic threat actor accessed some of our systems, including a system used for ordering and provisioning circuits, and exfiltrated some enterprise customer data," Bell told BleepingComputer. "Upon learning of the breach, we immediately contained the incident and secured our systems. There has been no impact to customer services." The company's description of the attacker as "agentic" suggests that AI-powered tools were used during the breach. Bell says it is sharing indicators of compromise (IOCs) and threat-hunting information with enterprise customers and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (CCCS). However, Bell has not publicly released the indicators of compromise and has not responded to BleepingComputer's request to share them so other organizations can check their environments for related activity. Bell told BleepingComputer that it has not yet identified the threat actor responsible for the attack. "We currently do not know the attribution," Bell said. Bell has not disclosed how many enterprise customers were impacted or the total amount of data stolen. In its customer notification, Bell urged organizations to remain cautious of unsolicited requests and social engineering attempts by individuals impersonating the telecommunications provider. history.title: Vendor data breach exposes Chase, Visa, Mastercard customer info
history.text: J.P. Morgan Chase warned it suffered a data breach after a cyberattack at a third-party service provider exposed customers' personal information and marketing data. The bank said the incident didn't disrupt its services and is unrelated to a service disruption that occurred earlier this week. "We have learned that third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyber attack," reads the firm's announcement on X. "Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses." J.P. Morgan Chase Bank is the largest U.S. bank by assets, with about $4.1 trillion as of June 2026. Its consumer banking division reports about 78 million active digital customers. Visa and Mastercard separately confirmed third-party incidents in statements to the media, though they have not confirmed any impact on customers. The two firms are major global payment network operators with presence in more than 200 countries, handling annual transaction volumes of multiple trillion USD. "Visa is aware of these claims. They are associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia Pacific," a Visa spokesperson told BleepingComputer. "Visa's systems were not involved and were not impacted. No payments data such as card numbers were affected. This is unrelated to any of the system disruptions across different industries this past week." Mastercard told BleepingComputer that they "were recently informed of an incident at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information – from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program." Mastercard's spokesperson assured that "There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards." "At this time, the exposure has been contained and our teams are working with the provider to support the impacted cardholders as needed." n0n ransomware claims the attack On November 11, 2026, the n0n ransomware group claimed responsibility for an attack on Qubole, suspected to be the third-party provider the payment services use. Qubole is a cloud data analytics company owned by Idera, used for cloud data analytics, automated processing, real-time analysis, and reporting. Between October 14 and 26, 2026, the hackers used compromised Qubole credentials to access customers' AWS environments through IAM roles the companies had previously configured to grant Qubole access. Allegedly, they stole 53.9 GB across 30,743 files directly from Qubole, including customer contracts, pricing records, staff and trial-user information, and production data. Additionally, they claimed to hold nearly one petabyte of data from Qubole's customer networks. n0n leaked the claimed Chase, Visa, and Mastercard data on its extortion site on November 16, 2026. The hacking group claimed it contacted Qubole and some of the affected companies before public reports from Sentra and Wiz detailed the attacks, but their extortion demands were ignored. history.title: Still tracking company passwords in spreadsheets? You’re flying blind.
history.text: The password spreadsheet your admins use may look like a complete inventory, but it only reflects some of the credentials employees have reported using. More specifically, that spreadsheet doesn’t show passwords that have been changed, created, or shared since the document was last updated, until someone brings it up to date. That’s assuming someone ever does. Meanwhile, work passwords can end up in all kinds of places. Someone saves one in their browser. A teammate sends a shared login in chat to move forward with a project. Another employee decides to put a few passwords in a personal vault because getting access to the company one takes too long. Unless someone reports these actions, the spreadsheet won’t capture them. And so, admins may think they have a handle on company credentials when, in fact, their spreadsheet tells only part of the story. The real reason credentials slip out of admins’ view The predominant factor is convenience. When the approved process is slow or unclear, employees use what’s at hand: a browser’s built-in password storage, a shared Google document, a Slack message, or one of the sticky notes on their desk. They may know that that’s against the rules, but in the moment, their priority is getting work done. That’s why a process that relies on employees to manually report every new password, update, and shared credential is nearly impossible to sustain. If the official route feels like an obstacle rather than the easiest way to access work tools, people are more likely to work around it. This preference for convenience shows up in people’s password habits, too. Verizon’s 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report found that, in the median case, only 49% of users’ passwords across different services were unique. In other words, more than half of those passwords were reused. The “TOP 20 Not-So-Secret Business Passwords” report by NordPass has also found “123456” to be the world’s most common password used in a corporate setting. This shows that people generally take the easy route when it comes to passwords. Without visibility, a company may not even know that one of its most important assets is protected by “123456” or another weak password. To solve this problem, organizations need an approach that works for both employees and admins. Without one, credentials can remain scattered and difficult to manage, increasing the risk created by those blind spots. The risks of poor visibility into company credentials When admins can’t see where work credentials are stored, they also cannot know who uses them, who they’ve been shared with, or whether they’ve changed. They also cannot assess the strength and reuse of the passwords employees rely on every day. Verizon’s report found that only 3% of compromised passwords in its dataset met basic complexity standards. That finding doesn’t describe every password in an organization, but it shows why teams need a way to identify weak credentials in the systems they manage. Reuse matters, too: if a password is compromised, reusing it across services can put more than one account at risk. This leads us to the most important element, which is that credentials still remain one of the main ways attackers gain unauthorized access to company systems and data. The 2026 edition of the Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report identified credential abuse as the initial access vector in 13% of breaches. It also found that vulnerability exploitation accounted for 31% of breaches, underscoring the need for credential protection as part of a broader security strategy. Keeping company credentials in a spreadsheet creates another risk. If ransomware attackers gain a foothold in the company network, they may search specifically for files containing passwords. Ransomware groups such as Pysa have used automated scripts to scan drives for filenames and folders containing terms like “password,” “login,” “pwd,” and “passwd.” If attackers find a spreadsheet, they may encrypt it and demand a ransom. They could also use the credentials inside to access other accounts and systems, potentially spreading the attack further. The solution? A structured approach that’s easy for admins to manage and for employees to follow. To keep company accounts protected, admins should be able to answer a few questions about each company password: Is it strong? Who owns it? Where is it stored? Who has access to it? Is it reused, old, or exposed in a breach? Each factor matters because any one of them can create risk. A strong password could still be reused across multiple accounts, so if it’s exposed in a breach, attackers may be able to use it to access those other accounts, too. A recent password change won’t tell you whether the right people still have access, either. Reviewing factors like these helps admins understand what needs attention. But how can they keep track of all of it? The right password manager can make this easier by giving your team one place to store and manage work credentials. NordPass, for example, offers organizations a centralized vault protected by XChaCha20 encryption and a zero-knowledge architecture, which means the service provider can’t access what’s stored inside. NordPass also helps admins check the credentials in the vault. With features like the Data Breach Scanner and Password Health, it can quickly identify weak, reused, old, and exposed passwords. With NordPass, admins can also set password requirements to make sure all credentials used by employees are strong, while users can share credentials securely over protected channels. Beyond that, the Sharing Hub feature shows who has access to passwords shared with multiple people or teams, and the activity log records actions related to company passwords. All of this gives admins a way to spot credential issues early, decide what to address first, and check what changed afterward to make sure company logins are as secure as they can be. Get a clear view of your company passwords with NordPass Make sure admins know where business credentials are stored, when they’re changed, and who can access them. At the same time, give employees quick, easy access to the tools they need without encouraging workarounds. Get started today What a managed vault won’t solve on its own A password manager can help solve the visibility problem, but it won’t address every aspect of it. Some employees may continue saving passwords in browsers or personal vaults, so adoption depends on making the approved option easy to use and setting clear expectations about how company logins should be handled. Shared accounts may need clearer ownership, too. Your IT team should decide who is responsible for each login, who needs access, and when that access should be removed. It’s also important to bear in mind that not every credential is a password. API keys, recovery codes, certificates, and other secrets may need their own storage, access, and ownership rules. Therefore, a password health report shouldn’t be treated as a complete inventory of every way employees access company resources. Stronger credential security starts beyond the spreadsheet A password spreadsheet or any other manually updated document can’t provide a reliable view of your company credentials. But a secure business password manager like NordPass can. It gives your team a secure place to store work credentials, shows you how healthy the passwords in the vault are, and makes it easier to set password requirements, share credentials securely, and track password-related activity. So, if you really want to know what’s happening with your company credentials, give NordPass a try, and replace the spreadsheet with a business password manager built for the job. Without visibility, companies face risks from compromised credentials, reuse across accounts, and ransomware attackers scanning for password files on networks.

history.title: In Other News: Norwegian Energy Firm Cyberattacks, Supercomputer Hack, New Nightmare Eclipse Exploit
history.text: SecurityWeek’s weekly cybersecurity news roundup offers a concise overview of important developments that may not receive full standalone coverage yet remain relevant to the broader threat landscape. This curated summary highlights key stories across vulnerability disclosures, emerging attack methods, policy updates, industry reports, and other noteworthy events to help readers stay well-informed about the evolving cybersecurity environment. Here are this week’s highlights: Gemini agents targeted Epoch AI AI evaluation firm Trajectory Labs says Gemini 4 Argon agents it stress-tested in October, with Gemini’s API safeguards turned on, tried to hack Epoch AI’s live website while hunting for answers to non-existent FrontierMath problems, attempting SQL injection and impersonating Epoch staff. Trajectory has paused all misalignment testing. Epoch says no private information was accessed. Google brings Gemini 4 Neon to defenders Google has released Gemini 4 Neon, a faster, lower-cost model for coding and enterprise work, and says a cyber-focused version will reach eligible members of its Fairwind Program for trusted defenders in the coming days. Google claims the model performs at frontier level across finding, validating and patching vulnerabilities. It also says Neon keeps Carbon-level safeguards against cyber and biosecurity misuse while turning down far fewer legitimate requests in those areas. Compromised migration vendor opens door to Infoblox data theft Networking and security company Infoblox has confirmed that hackers accessed certain company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor, which TechCrunch’s sources say handled SharePoint migration. The Register has since reported that the stolen files included NIOS configuration snapshots for some customers and personal details of employees and their dependents. Infoblox says it has no indication that its products, cloud services, software updates or build-and-release processes were involved. EU adds NoName057(16) to cyber sanctions list The Council of the EU has sanctioned 30 individuals and two entities over Russian information manipulation and cyber activity, including the Moscow-based Social Design Agency, 24 of its employees, and several pro-Kremlin propagandists. Under its cyber sanctions regime, the Council also listed NoName057(16), the pro-Russian group that has claimed attacks on government bodies, critical infrastructure and companies in Ukraine, the US and EU member states. Japanese supercomputer offline after intrusion Japan’s Riken research institute has suspended operations of the Fugaku supercomputer and cut off external access after detecting suspicious traffic on its user authentication system. In a November 17 notice, Riken said an outside party used a public dashboard showing Fugaku’s operational status to break into the system’s internal operations network and tamper with multiple servers. Names, email addresses and user IDs of up to 4,597 Fugaku and RIKYU users may have been exposed. Ukraine arrests ransomware suspects, 8-Digits member extradited to US Ukrainian police, working with the FBI, have arrested four alleged key members of a ransomware gang that posed as IT support in calls powered by an AI voice platform to obtain credentials or get remote access software installed. Separately, Kazakh national Roman Khlynovskiy has appeared in US court after being extradited from Italy over his alleged role in the 8-Digits Team, an INC and Lynx ransomware affiliate accused of stealing data from US hospitals, healthcare entities and schools and making over $500 million in ransom demands. In Florida, five people were arrested in a nationwide crackdown on account-takeover fraud schemes linked to more than $54 million in losses at over 65 US financial institutions. Test environment intrusion exposes Rakuten Securities customer data Japanese online brokerage Rakuten Securities says login IDs and branch codes for up to 11.25 million accounts, and personal and financial information for up to 4.47 million accounts, may have been exposed after attackers accessed a test environment system on November 11. The exposed details include names, dates of birth, addresses, employers, withdrawal bank account numbers, and declared annual income and financial assets. Equinor stops cyberattack as Skagerak Energi reports attempted intrusion Norwegian energy giant Equinor says it has stopped a cyberattack against some of its IT systems that it detected on November 17, adding that production was not affected and there is no sign that data was stolen or altered. The company said the attack was not a virus attack and did not appear to be specifically targeting it. A day after Equinor’s disclosure, Norwegian power company Skagerak Energi reported activity that may have been an attempted cyberattack on some of its IT systems, saying operations and production were not affected and there is no sign that information was leaked. Nightmare Eclipse drops unpatched Windows lock screen escape Researcher Nightmare Eclipse has published FastUnlock, an unpatched Windows 11 zero-day that abuses the Narrator screen reader to get past the lock screen and run code as the lock screen account. The attack requires physical access and at least one account linked to an online Microsoft account. Malware targets CACs left in personal computers The NSA says threat actors are using malware against the personal computers that Department of War (DoW) employees use with Common Access Card (CAC) readers. Once the malware has recorded the card’s PIN, it can use the CAC’s credentials to sign into federal and DoW websites for as long as the card stays in the reader. That often gives attackers access to anything the cardholder can normally reach. history.title: N-able says recent security breach led to major service outage
history.text: N-able says attackers who breached one of its servers have caused a major outage affecting Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud services worldwide. On Tuesday, the company initially blamed the outage on what it described as a "combination of platform configuration and service dependencies" affecting Mail Assure and SpamExperts services across the Americas, Asia-Pacific, and Europe. However, one day later, N-able disabled UI and API access and confirmed unauthorized access to a server in the Hosted Cloud environment. N-able also said the cyberattack didn't affect email flow or spam filtering and that it has yet to find evidence that the attackers gained access to customers' data and mailboxes. "Our earlier update said the disruption came from platform configuration and service dependencies and we believed we had remediated the issue. As we continued our investigation, we determined that the disruption was caused by a security incident affecting the Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud environment," the company said. "We are aware of unauthorized access to one of the servers in the Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud. We have taken steps to mitigate the threat and are continuing to harden our services to reduce the risk of recurrence. The investigation is ongoing, but at this time we do not have evidence that customer data was compromised, including access to tenants' mailboxes." After detecting the attack, N-able also alerted customers via email and took down the management portal (dashboard), as well as quarantine, logging, and mailbox synchronization supporting services. "Until these services are restored, customers may be unable to sign in to the control panel, view or release quarantined messages, review logs, or make configuration changes such as adding or removing domains," it added. N-able says this is unrelated to an N-central incident that forced it to take all hosted N-central environments offline to patch more than 30 zero-day flaws affecting its remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform. As BleepingComputer previously reported, hackers are now also exploiting a newly disclosed N-able zero-day vulnerability dubbed "4EverAble2Shell" to deploy cryptocurrency miners on vulnerable N-central servers. history.title: Industry Reactions to Major Outages and AI Patching Debate: Feedback Friday
history.text: A series of major technology outages have hit the United States, disrupting email, air travel, banking and government operations. The incidents included a nearly day-long Microsoft 365 outage, a nationwide FAA ground stop, a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase that slowed transactions at other banks, and an outage affecting the NSA’s classified internal network. United Airlines and Apple also experienced disruptions. Officials said there was no evidence of a cyberattack or a link between the incidents. Microsoft traced its outage to a months-old software defect, the FAA blamed a newly installed router, and the NSA cited routine maintenance. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, however, linked the NSA disruption to patching for a PHP vulnerability found with the help of AI. Sen. Mark Warner said AI-driven vulnerability discovery is pushing organizations to patch many systems at once, putting strain on infrastructure that wasn’t built for that pace of change. Industry professionals have commented on whether AI-accelerated patching played a role, the need for tested rollback plans, and the fragility of interconnected systems. And the feedback begins… Gil Tene, Chief Technology Officer & Co-founder, Azul: “We have strong reason to believe that AI-accelerated patch velocity is already causing major operational incidents. Based on direct experience with customers, we know that urgently deploying large, non-security-only OpenJDK updates does cause stability incidents. These rollouts sometimes fail and have to be reverted, leaving organizations exposed and delaying the remediation of the very vulnerabilities they are meant to address until teams find a workaround they can roll out without compromising stability. As AI accelerates the discovery of critical flaws, patch cycles are compressing rapidly. In the past four weeks alone, the Java community has had to absorb four update events, including three separate critical vulnerability events and a multitude of high-severity CVEs that couldn’t wait. When a critical Java vulnerability lands, teams must push OpenJDK updates into production within hours, often with less testing than they would normally do and with far more urgency to get the change rolled out before attackers can exploit it. When the fix for a vulnerability is available only as part of a much wider full update that brings along hundreds of unrelated changes, the rollout carries much more risk, because change is risk. The outage risk doesn’t come from the vulnerabilities themselves. It comes from the volume of change forced by compressed timelines. Hurried, urgent change is risky to begin with. The more change a hurried rollout carries, the greater the risk of instability and widespread incidents. Security-only updates minimize that risk by limiting the change to what is necessary to resolve the vulnerabilities, and nothing more.” Samuel Hassine, CEO and Co-founder, Filigran: “I think [faster patching pace driven by AI] plays a part, but I would be careful not to make it the whole story. From what has been made public so far, these outages look less like an AI problem than a change problem: updates and upgrades pushed onto systems that can’t take much change. AI is making that visible, because the list of flaws to fix now grows faster than most companies can safely roll out the fixes. For years our industry has told companies to patch faster and has measured them on that alone. But a fix that takes the service down is a security failure too, because being available is the first thing a customer expects from you. So the question I would put to every CEO is who owns the choice between leaving a flaw open a few more days and risking the service by closing it tonight. In most companies those are two teams with two different targets, and at this pace it has to be one person who answers for both.” Ken Barth, CEO, Catalogic Software: “AI is finding vulnerabilities faster than many remediation processes were built to handle. Microsoft fixed more than 1,400 vulnerabilities in its October security release, a monthly record, and 1,094 in November. The company has said AI-assisted discovery will put more fixes into each release. Each fix is a change to a live system. With the same staff and maintenance windows, a higher volume leaves less time to test each update, and less testing leaves more room for something to break. Nothing published so far links this pressure to the recent Microsoft 365 outage, but Microsoft’s own explanation shows how easily planned work can take a service down. Waiting longer is not a safe answer either. Google has reported attackers using AI to reverse-engineer patches and quickly build exploits for the flaws the patches address, so every published fix also tells attackers where to look. That makes being able to undo a change a security control in its own right. Before it reaches production, each update needs a verified restore point for the systems it touches, a tested rollback plan, and a clear owner for the decision to use it. The same discipline applies after something breaks. Microsoft restored services in stages to keep them stable, which is what careful recovery looks like. Organizations should know before the next incident which services must come back first, what each one depends on, and how long the full sequence takes. A recovery time that has never been tested is only an estimate, and boards should treat it as one.” Brian Contos, Field CISO, Mitiga: “Faster patching isn’t the problem by itself. AI is shrinking the time between a vulnerability being disclosed and being exploited, so defenders are under real pressure to ship fixes faster, and every change is a chance to break something. Look at the past week. Officials tied the FAA disruption to a network equipment upgrade, sources told CBS News the NSA outage followed routine patching, and JPMorgan Chase attributed its problems to a software issue. None of those appear to be attacks. What turns a routine change into a national outage is pushing it without being able to see its effects or quickly undo it. Speed is fine if every change is staged, watched for how the system behaves afterward and backed by a rollback someone has tested. The other lesson is how far a single failure travels. One router change at the FAA destabilized 17 of its 22 en route centers, and Chase said its issue may have slowed transactions at other banks. Redundancy alone doesn’t protect against a healthy component that’s misbehaving, because everything around it trusts it. Segmentation, independent failure domains and a rehearsed process for isolating a bad component quickly are what keep one problem from becoming everyone’s problem. The preparation for failures and cyberattacks is largely the same. An adversary can deliberately create these same disruptions, coordinate them across multiple locations and interfere with recovery. If a system can’t survive an accident, it won’t survive an adversary.” Benny Czarny, CEO and Founder, OPSWAT: “Faster patching can actually contribute to outages when testing and recovery cannot keep up. AI is increasing the pressure to fix vulnerabilities quickly, but you can’t attribute anything to AI without evidence from the investigation. Failures this week have resulted from cloning systems and their weaknesses along with them. When a primary system and its backup run the same software, receive the same update, and depend on the same network, then they really aren’t that independent. From a cybersecurity standpoint, critical infrastructure needs the same design mindset as an airplane cockpit, where primary and secondary systems use different hardware and software to reduce the chance that one defect disables every way of performing a critical function.” Bryson Byrd, Cybersecurity Advisor, Huntress: “Right now, there is no definitive link between these outages, and we should be careful about rushing to conclusions that AI or cyberattacks are responsible without having all the facts. What we do know is that there is a significant AI race going on between defenders and threat actors. As AI accelerates vulnerability discovery, defenders are under increasing pressure to engineer, test and push patches quickly to stay one step ahead. When companies are focused on speed of development, mistakes can happen. In the age of rapid patching, testing and verifying updates is arguably more important than ever. My concern is that these outages will cause organizations to start dialing back patches out of fear of being the next Microsoft or FAA. We cannot afford to go back to a time when system administrators could wait several days before deploying critical security updates. The window between vulnerability discovery and potential exploitation is shrinking, and slowing down patches could leave organizations exposed to threats they already know about. So we cannot stop updates or sacrifice testing for speed. We need to double down on resilience and make sure organizations are prepared when an update doesn’t go as planned. When it comes to critical patches and updates, there should always be a fallback plan in place, whether that’s a known, good backup or the last working code push that teams can quickly return to. We often see security teams with these plans documented, but the mechanisms haven’t actually been tested and verified to work. As infrastructure continues to evolve, these plans need to be tested regularly. Otherwise, when a bad update happens, organizations may not be prepared to respond, and a relatively contained issue can quickly grow into a much larger disruption.” Grayson North, Principal Threat Intelligence Consultant, GuidePoint Security: “This situation is a combination of increased media attention and a flurry of technical changes caused by AI’s rapid acceleration of vulnerability discovery. Outages are fairly common, but a few hours of downtime on a highly-visible system draws heightened attention. It can be compared to
history.summary: A series of major technology outages disrupted U.S. email, air travel, banking, and government operations, including a Microsoft 365 outage, a FAA ground stop, a JPMorgan Chase slowdown, and an NSA classified network outage. Officials found no evidence of cyberattack or link between the incidents, with Microsoft attributing its outage to a months-old software defect, the FAA blaming a newly installed router, and the NSA citing routine maintenance, though the Director of National Intelligence linked the NSA disruption to AI-patched PHP vulnerability work. Industry experts warned that AI-accelerated patching increases change velocity beyond infrastructure's capacity, emphasizing the need for tested rollback plans, staged rollouts, and better system segmentation to prevent single points of failure.

history.title: SBC Medical Group Data Breach Impacts Over 2 Million
history.text: California-based SBC Medical Group Holdings Incorporated (NASDAQ: SBC) has disclosed a data breach impacting over 2 million individuals in Japan. The medical services organization provides consulting, management, and operational support to medical corporations and clinics. Hackers accessed an online platform SBC Medical Group manages and compromised databases containing customer information associated with certain clinics in Japan, the company said in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). SBC Medical Group continues to investigate the attack but has confirmed that personal and medical information was likely compromised. The hackers stole the basic information of 1,624,000 individuals, including names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, dates of birth, gender, patient card numbers, member IDs, and survey responses. They also compromised the reservation-request information of 255,416 people, as well as the content entered in web inquiry forms by 217,769 individuals. According to the filing, 4,513 people also had their treatment descriptions and stored image file names stolen, while 15,007 had the basic information, treatment names, and review text exfiltrated. For 14 individuals, credit card information was also compromised. “The Company has confirmed that all of these credit cards were in a state in which additional payments could not be processed, such as having expired,” SBC Medical Group said. Additionally, the hackers stole customer passwords, along with 20,000 records containing employee names, IDs, and passwords. “For 459 employees, information provided at the time of employment, including bank account and pension-related information, withholding tax certificates and dependent exemption declarations, was also affected,” the company said. In a separate incident involving the third-party reservation service Tribeau, hackers accessed administrator accounts and accessed the information of approximately 19,000 individuals. For 12,641 of them, the threat actors compromised Kana names, phone numbers, age, and requested treatments. For three people, the hackers also accessed message contents, dates of birth, and gender, and for 6,804 they compromised reservation information and treatment details. “The operator confirmed that the obtained information was not linked to case or review information, including photographs, on Tribeau. Email addresses, residential addresses, credit card information, passwords, and electronic medical records were not included in that platform incident. The company and the provider continue to investigate the access and its cause,” the company said. SBC Medical Group said both incidents have been remediated. It isolated the affected server and evicted the hackers, and rotated the passwords for all the clinics to which it provides management services on Tribeau. “The company is continuing to assess the potential impact of the incidents on its business, financial condition and results of operations,” SBC Medical Group said. history.title: European Commission Confirms AI-Assisted Cyberattack Disrupted Services
history.text: The European Commission has confirmed falling victim to an AI-assisted cyberattack that disrupted several of its services. Hackers hit the European Union’s main executive body in late October, and the attack has been largely contained. The investigation into the incident continues, Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said during a press conference. “As a protective and preventive measure, we temporarily took down several applications, and most of them have since then been restored. We are taking any necessary steps based on the findings, as they come,” Regnier said. The attack was detected on October 22 and was confirmed on October 26. The investigation has found no evidence of a data breach affecting the Commission’s staff, Regnier added. According to Politico, the hackers potentially compromised large amounts of data and caused disruptions that lasted over 10 days. Impacted services included the Commission’s HR platform Sysper, medical reimbursement system MyPMO, and translation systems. While Regnier has confirmed that the hackers used an AI tool during the attack, he did not attribute the incident to a known group and said he was not aware of the Commission receiving a ransom demand related to the attack. Regnier has not named the AI tool used in the attack, but the disclosure came roughly two weeks after the European Union’s cybersecurity arm CERT-EU warned of threat actors using the AI-powered penetration-testing framework Artex to target its constituency. “We assess that Artex’s public availability will likely accelerate adoption by threat actors, resulting in more frequent, faster, and more scalable automated attacks with a higher success rate,” CERT-EU said. Artex is one of the AI frameworks that threat actors have been increasingly leveraging in attacks, and has been used to hack Barracuda, Railway, ConnectWise customers, and other organizations. history.title: Hackers Exploit Critical VMware, Cisco, and Apache Flaws as Espionage Attacks Emerge
history.text: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Friday added four flaws impacting Apache Roller, Cisco Expressway, SAP NetWeaver, and Broadcom VMware vCenter to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV), citing evidence of active exploitation. The vulnerabilities are listed below - - CVE-2026-129448 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A deserialization of untrusted data vulnerability in Apache Roller that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code via the XML-RPC endpoint, which accepts and deserializes vendor extension types before authentication. (Fixed in November 2026) - CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A use of hard-coded credentials vulnerability in Cisco Expressway Series that could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker with persistent cookies and network access to execute commands as root on a clustered device via the database service. (Fixed in October 2026) - CVE-2025-42884 (CVSS score: 6.5) - An improper neutralization of special elements in data query logic vulnerability in SAP NetWeaver Enterprise Portal that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to disclose or modify server information via injected JNDI environment properties or a URL used during JNDI lookup operations. (Fixed in November 2025) - CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An authentication bypass using an alternate path or channel vulnerability in VMware vCenter that could allow an unauthenticated attacker with network access to vCenter to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system. (Fixed in November 2026) Earlier this week, the maintainers of Apache Roller acknowledged that the "issue is being actively exploited" but did not reveal how it was being weaponized or who is behind it. As of writing, there also appear to be no public reports documenting active exploitation of CVE-2025-42884. The addition of CVE-2026-76466 to the KEV catalog follows a report from F6 that the vulnerability was exploited to breach a Russian organization following the release of a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit, enabling the attackers to move laterally across the network and access sensitive data. The activity has not been attributed to any threat actor. The exploitation of CVE-2026-123890, on the other hand, has linked to a suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group tracked as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221), which is said to have weaponized it in conjunction with another now-patched flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support (CVE-2026-102764, CVSS score: 9.3) to deploy custom backdoors for persistent access and data theft. Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies have been urged to patch all four vulnerabilities by November 23, 2026, pursuant to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk.

history.title: Microsoft Entra Connect Health flaw exploited to steal tenant data
history.text: Microsoft is warning organizations that it suffered a data breach after attackers exploited a vulnerability in its Entra Connect Health service to gain unauthorized access to administrator email addresses and tenant configuration information. Microsoft Entra Connect Health is a cloud-based monitoring service that allows administrators to monitor the health, performance, and alerts of their on-premises identity infrastructure through the Microsoft Entra admin center. According to a security notification sent to admins yesterday and shared on Reddit, Microsoft discovered the vulnerability in the Entra Connect Health API on November 9, 2026, after it was first introduced on July 23. An investigation determined that the flaw was exploited, allowing unauthorized parties to access tenant and service-monitoring metadata and potentially modify Connect Health monitoring configurations. "On 20 November 2026, we concluded our investigation and determined that unauthorized read-only access to tenant-level metadata associated with your organization had occurred. We did not identify any unauthorized configuration changes," Microsoft said in the notification. The company says the exposed information included: - Email addresses belonging to tenant technical contacts and administrator accounts. - Tenant IDs, display names, initial domain names, country codes, and regional information. - Microsoft Entra license tiers and directory synchronization status, including whether synchronization was enabled and the last synchronization timestamp. - Connect Health onboarding status. - An expired certificate previously used to register Connect Health agents with a Microsoft internal service that was decommissioned in late 2024. Microsoft says the expired certificate was no longer in use but remained in Connect Health storage and was still returned by the API. However, the company says the vulnerability did not expose user passwords, password hashes, authentication tokens, valid cryptographic keys, on-premises server and Active Directory topology details, or Azure subscription information. Microsoft deployed a server-side fix on November 19 to prevent further exploitation and reviewed available telemetry to identify unauthorized API calls affecting customers. The company finished its investigation on November 20 and began notifying affected organizations. Microsoft has not disclosed how many organizations were impacted, but more than a dozen administrators have reported receiving the notification in the Reddit post. Some managed service providers (MSPs) also reported receiving notifications for multiple customer tenants, with one administrator saying the emails arrived hours apart. The notification says no software updates or other customer remediation are required to address the vulnerability. However, Microsoft recommends that organizations alert their security teams to potential targeted phishing and social-engineering attacks that could target the exposed administrator email addresses and tenant information. Organizations are also advised to ensure privileged accounts use phishing-resistant multifactor authentication, review their Connect Health configurations, and examine Microsoft Entra audit and sign-in logs for suspicious activity. Microsoft also published a PowerShell script at https://aka.ms/ConnectHealth/scripts that allows administrators to view the types of tenant metadata that could have been exposed. However, the script displays current configuration values rather than the information that was accessed during the breach. Microsoft has not disclosed who exploited the vulnerability, how many tenants were impacted, or when the attacks first began. When contacted by BleepingComputer, Microsoft confirmed that it had fixed the vulnerability and notified impacted customers. "We identified and addressed a security issue affecting Microsoft Entra Connect Health that could have resulted in unauthorized access to tenant-level contact and configuration metadata. We deployed a fix on November 19, 2026, and have notified impacted customers through Azure Service Health, providing guidance and support," a Microsoft spokesperson told BleepingComputer. history.title: FBI reportedly hacked again, this time targeting nationwide police database
history.text: FBI systems have reportedly been breached for the second time in two months, this time targeting the agency's National Crime Information Center (NCIC), which is used to share information between local, state, and federal law enforcement agencies. The National Crime Information Center is an FBI-operated database used by law enforcement agencies across the United States to share information about wanted and missing persons, outstanding arrest warrants, stolen vehicles and firearms, protection orders, and other criminal justice records. Police officers routinely use the system during traffic stops, criminal investigations, and background checks. According to CNN's reporting, the FBI is investigating an apparent breach of the NCIC system, citing two people briefed on the investigation. The intrusion was reportedly discovered in recent days, although it is unclear when the breach occurred, how the attackers gained access, or whether any information was stolen. The FBI has not publicly confirmed the incident and did not respond to CNN's request for comment. The reported breach comes just two months after the ShinyHunters extortion group claimed to have breached the FBI's systems by exploiting an unpatched Oracle PeopleSoft vulnerability. The earlier attack targeted a third-party platform associated with the FBI's recruitment website, FBIJobs.gov, with ShinyHunters claiming to have stolen sensitive information from the agency's systems. The FBI subsequently launched an investigation that led to the arrests of suspected ShinyHunters members, including a Canadian cybersecurity executive reportedly linked to the attacks. There is currently no indication that the latest NCIC incident is connected to ShinyHunters or the earlier breach. It remains unclear whether the attackers accessed sensitive law enforcement records stored in NCIC or whether the intrusion affected the system's availability to law enforcement agencies. BleepingComputer contacted the FBI on Friday evening with questions about the reported breach but has not received a response.
